lines.text: Zoom into one candle on a stock chart, and you'll find a war inside.
Every price is a shelf. Above the price, sell orders wait: people who'll sell, but only at their price. Below it, buy orders wait.
The price only moves when someone stops waiting. A buyer who wants in right now eats the cheapest sell orders on the shelf.
Clear a whole shelf, and the price steps up to the next one. Shelf by shelf, the candle fills green.
Now sellers rush in. They eat the buy orders below, and the green starts to drain.
Eat all the way past the open, and the candle closes red.
And the wick? It's the highest shelf the buyers reached, before the sellers dragged it back.
Now the smart part. Big players can't just buy a million shares. There aren't enough sellers on the shelves.
So where do they find sellers? Right here. Just under the obvious low, where everyone's stop loss sits. Every stop is a sell order, waiting to fire.
They push the price down through that line. The stops fire, a flood of sellers hits the shelves, and the big player buys every share.
Order filled. The selling dries up, and the price rips back up. That's a liquidity sweep.
It works upside down too. Above the obvious high, the stops of short sellers are buy orders, waiting to be swept.
How to spot one: a fast wick through an obvious level, then a strong close right back inside.
This isn't financial advice. Trade small, and never park your stop exactly where the crowd does.
